new_statements.quote: However, in longer constructions (of several clauses) basic and secondary tone distinctions tend to disappear. They are replaced by a phrase level phenomena. This is realized as a raising of pitch and an increase in intensity on the ultima or penult of the intonation phrase and can be termed primary stress. If the phrase ends in (1) a syllable with basic high tone, (2) a syllable with changing tone (some prepositions, for example) or (3) a phrase terminator expletive (cf., 2.2.5.3), this will carry the primary stress. If the final syllable has a non-changing low basic tone (nde "he, she, it", for example) the primary stress will be realized on the syllable preceding it, that is the phrase penult.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kapsiki is analysed as a two-tone (H/L) language with light tonal load; Smith describes no lexical word stress. Prominence ('primary stress' = raised pitch plus greater intensity) is assigned at the level of the intonation phrase: it falls on the phrase-final syllable when that syllable bears basic high tone, a changing tone, or is a phrase-terminating expletive, and otherwise (final syllable with plain low tone) on the phrase penult. In connected speech this phrase stress largely supersedes the tone distinctions heard in short utterances; Smith suggests the language is shifting from tone toward a stress-intonation type.
new_statements.secondary_stress: According to Mohrlang 1974 (fn. 1, summarising the same pages), Smith 'goes on to describe a type of secondary stress which occurs with non-final high tones'; Smith's own wording of this was not recoverable from snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: Placement is tone-conditioned: final syllables with non-changing low tone (e.g. the pronoun nde) push primary stress to the penult; 'changing-tone' items (some prepositions) and phrase-terminator expletives attract it. In short utterances/isolation, basic and secondary tone patterns rather than stress are heard.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the intonation phrase (ultima or penult of the phrase), not the word; described for longer constructions of several clauses. Citation forms show tone, not stress. Text obtained only as Google Books snippets (verbatim, saved), not from a full copy; the clause 'increase in intensity on the ultima or penult of the intonation' is attested in Mohrlang 1974's verbatim quotation of Smith and is consistent with the adjoining Smith snippets ('...raising of pitch and an' / 'phrase and can be termed primary stress').
new_statements.identity_note: Smith 1969 describes 'Kapsiki' as spoken around Mogodé, Cameroon = Psikye proper (psik1239, ISO kvj). Mohrlang 1974 calls it 'Kapsiki, a Higi dialect in North Cameroun'; his own first-hand stress statement ('stress is predictable and seems to be a feature of vowel length; high tone syllables tend to have more stress') concerns Higi/Kamwe of Nkafa (kamw1239), not Psikye, and should not be transferred.
